questions.q: During election campaigns, political parties present and elaborate on their:
options: agenda and promises
candidates' educational certificates only
court judgments
annual budget documents
questions.explanation: Parties present their agenda and elaborate on their promises in election rallies, and discuss issues through various media platforms, helping voters understand what each party stands for.
questions.fact: They present their agenda, elaborate on their promises in election rallies, and discuss and debate on issues through various media platforms.

questions.q: Which of the following is mentioned in the chapter as a challenge to free and fair elections?
options: Excessive rainfall on polling day
Misinformation and fake news
Too many polling stations in cities
Very long parliamentary terms
questions.explanation: Misinformation, fake news and intimidation are listed among the challenges that the ECI addresses through the RPAs, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, VVPAT and awareness campaigns.
questions.fact: For challenges such as misinformation, fake news, intimidation, etc., the ECI addresses them through RPA 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, VVPAT, and voters' awareness campaigns.

questions.q: Under the Anti-Defection Law, what can happen to a member who voluntarily gives up their party membership?
options: The member must pay a heavy fine
The member can be disqualified from the House
The member loses citizenship
Nothing, as the law is only advisory
questions.explanation: The Anti-Defection Law allows the disqualification of a member of Parliament or a State Assembly who voluntarily gives up party membership or votes against the party's whip.
questions.fact: If a member of the Parliament or a State Assembly voluntarily gives up their party membership or votes against the party's instructions (whip), the member can be disqualified from the respective House.

questions.q: Which of the following is a condition for recognition as a NATIONAL party?
options: Winning at least one seat in the Lok Sabha
Securing 6% of votes in one state
Being recognised as a State Party in at least four states
Contesting elections in at least two states
questions.explanation: One criterion for national party status is being recognised as a State Party in at least four states; other routes include 6% of votes in four or more states plus four Lok Sabha seats, or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states.
questions.fact: It is recognised as a State Party at least in four states (a criterion for national party recognition).
questions.hint: National recognition is linked to a party's presence across several states.

questions.q: A party can be recognised as a state party by securing not less than a certain percentage of the valid votes polled in the State, without any additional seat condition. What is this percentage?
questions.explanation: Under the state party recognition criteria, securing not less than 8% of the valid votes polled in the State, in a Lok Sabha or Legislative Assembly general election, is itself sufficient; the 6% criteria additionally require winning seats.
questions.fact: Secures not less than 8% of the valid votes polled in the State at a General Election to the Lok Sabha from the State or to the Legislative Assembly of the State.
questions.hint: This is the highest vote-share percentage among the state party criteria.

questions.q: Against the backdrop of which event did various parties unite as the Janata Party in 1977?
options: The National Emergency
The Kargil War
The Non-Cooperation Movement
The Quit India Movement
questions.explanation: In 1977, against the backdrop of the National Emergency of 1975-77, various political parties came together as the Janata Party, which formed the first coalition government at the national level.
questions.fact: It was in 1977 that various political parties formed an alliance as the Janata Party against the backdrop of the National Emergency (1975-77).

questions.q: In the chapter's case study, the wall writings and campaign posters pasted the day before the assembly elections are examples of violations of:
options: The Anti-Defection Law
The Model Code of Conduct
The Representation of the People Act, 1950
The Delimitation Commission's orders
questions.explanation: Ishani's case study asks readers to spot Model Code of Conduct violations; wall writings, posters and pamphlets put up right before polling day are such violations, which can be reported through the cVIGIL app.
questions.fact: The case study shows wall writing and campaign posters pasted everywhere the day before the elections and cites them as examples of violations of the Model Code of Conduct.

questions.q: India's multi-party system reflects the country's rich diversity of languages, cultures, religions and regions.
questions.explanation: India has a multi-party system in which many parties exist and compete in elections, and this plurality mirrors the country's social and regional diversity.
questions.fact: India has a multi-party system, which means that many political parties exist and compete in elections. This system reflects the country's rich diversity of languages, cultures, religions, and regions.

questions.q: Defection is always viewed as political opportunism and can never be seen as upholding conscience.
questions.explanation: While defection is often seen as political opportunism that harms party discipline and stability, the chapter notes it can also be viewed as a way to uphold conscience or respond to changing public expectations.
questions.fact: On the contrary, defection can also be viewed as a way to uphold conscience or respond to changing public expectations.

questions.q: Under the Anti-Defection Law, the Speaker or Chairman of the House decides what needs to be done in defection cases.
questions.explanation: When a member is accused of defection, it is the Speaker or the Chairman of the concerned House who decides what needs to be done in the matter.
questions.fact: The Speaker or Chairman of the House decides what needs to be done in such cases.

questions.q: A member who votes against the party's instructions in the legislature is said to have defied the ___.
questions.explanation: The whip is the party's instruction on how its members should vote in the legislature; voting against it can lead to disqualification under the Anti-Defection Law.
questions.fact: If a member votes against the party's instructions (whip), the member can be disqualified from the respective House.

questions.q: Abandoning or switching from the political party under whose banner a candidate was elected is called ___.
questions.explanation: Defection means leaving the party on whose ticket a legislator was elected, either by joining another party or by acting independently of the party's decisions in the legislature.
questions.fact: Defection refers to abandoning or switching from the political party under whose banner the candidate was elected.

questions.q: India has a ___-party system in which many political parties exist and compete in elections.
questions.explanation: In a multi-party system like India's, many parties contest elections, offering voters a wide range of choices and reflecting the country's diversity.
questions.fact: India has a multi-party system, which means that many political parties exist and compete in elections.

questions.q: Match each party or alliance with its description.

pairs.r: Formed the first coalition government at the national level
Alliance led by the Bharatiya Janata Party
Alliance led by the Indian National Congress until its 2023 dissolution
Parties lacking vote share or that never contested after registration
Recognised on the basis of its performance within one state

questions.explanation: The Janata Party of 1977 was the first national coalition; the NDA is BJP-led and the UPA was INC-led until 2023; RUPPs are registered but unrecognised, while state parties earn recognition through performance in one state.
questions.fact: The Janata Party formed the first coalition government at the national level; since the late 1990s the NDA (led by BJP) and the UPA (led by INC until 2023) have been the major alliances.

questions.q: Match each provision or officer with its role.

pairs.r: Mandates the establishment of a Delimitation Commission
Provide for the ECI and define its powers and duties
Supervises election work at the State level
State Government officer who can be assigned election duties

questions.explanation: Article 82 sets up delimitation, Articles 324-329 create the ECI, the CEO supervises state-level election work, officers like District Magistrates are drafted for election duty, and 25 January is National Voters' Day.
questions.fact: Article 82 mandates a Delimitation Commission; Articles 324 to 329 provide for the ECI; the CEO supervises state election work; officers like DMs are assigned election duties; 25 January is National Voters' Day.

questions.q: Arrange these events in the correct chronological order.
orderItems: End of the era of single-party dominated elections (1967)
Janata Party alliance formed against the National Emergency (1977)
NDA and UPA became major alliances (late 1990s)
UPA dissolved and reconstituted under a new name (2023)
questions.explanation: Single-party dominance ended in 1967, the Janata alliance came together in 1977, the NDA and UPA dominated from the late 1990s, and the UPA was dissolved and reconstituted in 2023.
questions.fact: The year 1967 witnessed an end to single-party dominated elections; the Janata alliance came in 1977; NDA and UPA have been major alliances since the late 1990s; the UPA was dissolved in 2023.

questions.q: Arrange the events of Ishani's first voting experience in the correct order.
orderItems: Ishani registers to vote through the ECI's online portal
She goes to the polling station with her mother and brother
A wheelchair is made available for her disabled brother
questions.explanation: Ishani first registered online, then reached the polling station where a wheelchair was arranged for her brother, after which she cast her vote and finally saw the VVPAT slip.
questions.fact: Ishani registered to vote through the ECI's online portal; at the polling station a wheelchair was made available; after casting her vote she was able to see the VVPAT slip.

questions.q: Select all correct: what do political parties do in a democracy, according to the chapter?
options: Appointing the Election Commissioners
Organising public opinion
Campaigning on specific issues
Offering voters meaningful choices
questions.explanation: Political parties organise public opinion, campaign on specific issues, offer voters meaningful choices and enable informed decisions; they do not appoint Election Commissioners.
questions.fact: Political parties organise public opinion, campaign on specific issues, offer voters meaningful choices, and enable voters to make informed decisions.

questions.q: Select all correct: the ECI addresses challenges to free and fair elections through —
options: The Model Code of Conduct
Banning all political parties
EVMs and VVPAT
Voters' awareness campaigns
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the RPAs, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, VVPAT and voters' awareness campaigns as the ECI's tools against challenges like misinformation and intimidation; banning parties is not among them.
questions.fact: The ECI addresses challenges through RPA 1950 and 1951, the Model Code of Conduct, EVMs, Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT), voters' awareness campaigns, and other measures.

questions.q: Select all correct: which statements describe Registered Unrecognised Political Parties (RUPP)?
options: Parties that have not secured enough percentage of votes in elections
Parties that have never contested elections since their registration
Parties recognised as national parties in four states
Parties appointed by the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: RUPPs are registered parties that either failed to secure enough vote percentage in Legislative Assembly or General Elections, or have never contested elections since their registration.
questions.fact: RUPP are the parties that have not secured enough percentage of votes in the Legislative Assembly or the General Elections, and parties that have never contested elections since their registration.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the Anti-Defection Law is INCORRECT?
options: The Anti-Defection Law was passed in 1985 through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act.
Under the law, the President of India personally decides defection cases.
The purpose of the law is to prevent defection and provide stability to the elected government.
A member who votes against the party's whip can be disqualified from the House.
questions.explanation: Defection cases are decided by the Speaker or the Chairman of the House, not by the President; the other statements correctly describe the law passed in 1985 through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act.
questions.fact: The Speaker or Chairman of the House decides what needs to be done in defection cases.

questions.q: Which of these statements about party recognition is INCORRECT?
options: Every party that registers with the ECI is automatically recognised as a national party.
A party recognised as a State Party in at least four states can gain national party status.
One national party criterion is winning at least 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states.
A party can be recognised as a state party by securing not less than 8% of valid votes polled in the state.
questions.explanation: Registration with the ECI does not automatically bring recognition; parties that fail the vote and seat criteria remain Registered Unrecognised Political Parties (RUPP).
questions.fact: Registered Unrecognised Political Parties are those that have not secured enough percentage of votes or have never contested elections since registration.

questions.q: Which of these statements about coalition politics is INCORRECT?
options: In 1977, parties united as the Janata Party against the backdrop of the National Emergency.
The Janata Party formed the first coalition government at the national level.
The era of single-party dominated elections in India ended in 1989.
Since the late 1990s, the NDA and the UPA have been major political alliances.
questions.explanation: The era of single-party dominated elections ended in 1967, when the era of alliances began, not in 1989; the Janata Government of 1977 was the first national coalition.
questions.fact: The year 1967 witnessed an end to the era of single-party dominated elections in India and an era of alliances began.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Anti-Defection Law provides stability to the elected government.
Reason (R): A member who voluntarily gives up party membership or votes against the whip can be disqualified from the House.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A: the possibility of disqualification discourages members from abandoning their parties, which prevents defection and stabilises the elected government.
questions.fact: The purpose of the law is to prevent defection, thereby providing stability to the elected government; a member who defects can be disqualified from the House.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Voters learn about candidates and their policies primarily through political parties.
Reason (R): Most candidates in elections contest as independents without any party affiliation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: A is true because parties are the main source of information about candidates' policies and visions, but R is false, since most candidates belong to a political party and only some contest independently.
questions.fact: Voters learn about candidates, their policies and their vision primarily through the political parties; most candidates belong to a political party, though some contest independently.
